name: Signal red
lede: Signal red is a vivid red named for warning lights, and also a trade name for the synthetic pigment para red and for vermilion substitutes.

sections.title: Two meanings
sections.body:
Paterson defines the term as a vivid red, and notes that coloured lights are used on railways as warning signals, in preference to semaphore signals [1]. That is the modern sense.

In the pigment trade the name has another sense. The Pigment Compendium lists signal red as a synonym of para red, which is a pigment classed as Colour Index 12070 or Pigment Red 1 and introduced in 1885 [2]. It lost most of its importance because of its deficiencies [2]. By Heaton's account in 1928, signal red was also a variety of vermilionette, a family of substitutes for [[vermilion]] made by precipitating dyes such as eosin [2][3]. Other names in that family were royal red and Victoria red [3].

sections.title: Which red?
sections.body: Our swatch, #E72512, is a bright orange-leaning red [4]. The library's other Signal Red, the RAL 3001 industrial standard, is much darker, about #A02128 on screen, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the name in block 11 [4]. Maerz and Paul first recorded the name in 1902 [4]. Near neighbors are [[tomato-red]], [[scarlet]] and [[carmine]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, 15 contain this red over at least five per cent of the canvas, within six units [5]. Seven are from the 1800s and three from the 1900s, and six are Spanish [5]. A 1935 table scene by Bonnard is among them [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so this is a color match and not a pigment test [5].
